title_zh: 答应的工作，最后怎样算数？
deck_zh: 威斯康星与富士康的招商协议：愿景、合同、核验结果，以及计划改变之后，谁还能继续问。
deck_en: Wisconsin and Foxconn: a public promise becomes a contract, then a verified count. What should survive when the plan changes?

historical_note_zh: 本文读到2025年11月25日 WEDC 的扩建公告，其中核验数字截至2024年12月31日；不据此宣布2025年底目标是否完成，也不核算全部州与地方成本。2018年审计报告18-18通过 WEDC 2019年1月董事会材料中的原文核对，页码采用报告自身页码。税收抵免上限、取得资格与实际支付分别处理，不作现行投资或税务建议。
historical_note_en: This essay follows the record through WEDC's 25 November 2025 expansion announcement, whose verified figures are dated 31 December 2024. It does not determine whether the end-2025 target was met or calculate all state and local costs. Audit report 18-18 was checked in its original reproduction within WEDC's January 2019 board materials; references use the report's printed pages. Credit ceilings, eligibility and payment remain distinct. This is not current investment or tax advice.
body_zh: 一个地方添了多少份工作，才算等到了当初答应的未来？
如果只读招商新闻，这个问题仿佛很容易。投资多少，创造多少岗位，名字旁边各有一个数字。可真正难的时候，往往是在几年以后：工厂确实有了，工人也确实在上班，做的东西却变了，合同改过了，新闻里的数字还在继续长。此时说一句全成功或全失败，都太容易。
富士康在美国威斯康星州的项目，值得慢一点读。我们不必替当年的掌声辩护，也不必把后来留下的一切说成空无。先把同一个问题问得具体些：哪一个承诺，由谁在什么时候核验；达不到时，什么可以改变，什么不能悄悄翻篇？
## 愿景到了合同里，会变成什么
2017年11月，威斯康星经济发展公司 WEDC 与富士康签订十五年协议。2019年董事会材料回顾的规模是：最多一百亿美元投资、最多一万三千个岗位，以及最高二十八点五亿美元的绩效税收抵免。这最后一个数，是附条件的抵免额度，不是签约当天已经交给企业的现金。[1]
这类安排有一种可以理解的吸引力。一家大型制造企业到来，可能使培训、供应商和基础设施的投入有了彼此配合的机会。政府愿意分担一部分早期风险，并不天然荒唐。企业也需要看得见的条件，才能安排自己的设备、订单和人员。光喊不要干预，不能代替对具体支持方式的判断。
但一万三千个岗位究竟在协议里怎样算数？立法审计局2018年的报告指出：合同规定的最低岗位规模与一万三千并不是同一个数。报告说明，在最后一个合同年度，按相应工资水平计算，一万零四百个岗位也可能取得该年度全部可用的岗位抵免。工资和岗位一起进入公式，不能只拿宣传数字去读付款条件。[1]
这并不证明谁在签字时存心骗人。它说明，普通人听见的未来与行政机关真正执行的条件之间，可能隔着一段很长的细则。想判断支持是否值得，第一步不是挑一个最大的数字，而是看愿景怎样被写进了可执行的义务。没写进去的部分，又由谁承担落空的风险？
审计报告还发现了另一种缝隙：WEDC 的政策说，年度岗位未达最低要求时，相关未发放抵免不能结转；实际合同却允许岗位抵免继续结转。WEDC 当时表示，准备修改政策，使之与合同一致。这里准备改的是政策，并不能写成审计已经迫使企业接受更严格的合同。[1]
这处细节没有剪彩热闹，却十分要紧。一个机构既要促成项目，也要解释项目是否合格，它自己的执行方法同样需要被别人查看。只核查企业报来的数，不核查审核者怎样把数算出来，问责仍可能漏掉半边。
对公共支持的信任，不应只靠某个人保证自己会严格把关。居民应该能够沿着文件，找到从承诺到资格、从资格到给付的每一步。支持做得越大，这条路越不该只留给熟悉合同的人走。
## 允许改变，不等于改写记忆
项目后来调整。2021年4月，州政府宣布重新谈妥协议：绩效税收抵免上限改为八千万美元，期限由十五年缩短为六年，投资和岗位目标也重新设置。公告还说，不再限定必须生产某一种产品，只要满足投资与雇用条件，就可以按规定取得激励。[2]
企业一方给出的理由是经济条件变化，需要灵活回应市场；州方则强调减少纳税人承担的额度，同时保住已有公共投入的用途。这两种理由都应被认真听取。订单和技术不会为了维护一份旧新闻稿而停止变化，把企业永远钉在最初产品上，也可能让实际工作更难留下来。[3]
然而，允许改计划与认为旧计划已经兑现，是两件事。一个新协议可以为接下来提供更合适的条件，却不能反过来证明，最初那次选择原本就恰到好处。今天怎样处理已有厂房，与当年是否应该按那样的规模支持，应当分别讨论。
2021年的公告把新旧州级抵免上限之差，称为节省二十七点七亿美元。读到这里，最好停一下：缩减尚未全部兑现的最高额度，不等于收回同样多已经花掉的钱，更不能从这个差额推出全部地方基础设施成本也一并消失了。[2]
反过来，不能因为另有地方投入，就把原来的抵免上限全部记作已经支付。这会把两种错误叠在一起。要问代价，得继续逐项读土地、道路、融资和税收安排；本篇没有完成那笔总账，也不拿一个醒目的除法，宣布每份工作的全部公共成本。
这里真正令人为难的，是已经投入之后的判断。继续支持，可能仍有理由；停下来，也可能有理由。可如果每次都只说已经花了这么多，不能不继续，那么最早那次承诺便会变成一道门，后来的每次决定都只能从同一边出去。
要让重新谈判仍然是一种选择，就得容许有人问：新增的这一笔支持，今天还能带来什么？若不再给，后果又是什么？这些问题不等于反对工人有工作，也不等于希望厂房闲置。恰恰是因为真实的生计已经在那里，新的决定才值得比旧口号更仔细。
## 把未来与已经发生的事分开
2025年11月25日，WEDC 又发布扩建公告。先别急着看标题里的新投资。公告内部给出了一组有明确日期的结果：截至2024年12月31日，WEDC 核验投资接近七点一七亿美元，创造岗位一千二百四十二个，符合取得六千二百九十万美元税收抵免的条件。[4]
这些不是一片空白。设备、投入和岗位，至少在这份核验口径下确实存在。它们也不是一万三千个岗位的另一种说法。承认目前留下了什么，与追问当年期待的差距，可以同时进行，不必先把一边抹掉。
时间也要对齐。2025年公告回顾的旧目标，是到2025年12月31日达到一千四百五十四个岗位。用2024年底的一千二百四十二，直接宣布2025年底目标未完成，就把相差一年的两个时点硬拼在一起了。我们手里这份公告本身不能给出那个年终结论。[4]
同样，符合抵免条件，不等于本文已经核实同额现金全部支付；企业在当地创造岗位，也不等于证明这些岗位全由补贴带来。若没有这项激励，会有多少投资仍然发生，其他企业又会怎样发展，需要别的证据。核验可以回答有没有达到约定口径，不能单独回答整项政策是否划算。
接着才读未来。新公告提出再投资五点六九亿美元、未来四年新增一千三百七十四个岗位；州级绩效抵免总上限增至九千六百万美元，延至2029年底。公告所列的总岗位目标为二千六百一十六个。这些是新阶段的承诺与条件，不能和前一段已核验结果混写成已经实现。[4]
新闻需要向前看，这可以理解。但公共账本还得允许向后看。若每个新目标都把旧目标挤走，读者便只能反复参加下一次出发，永远等不到上一段旅程怎样结束。好的更新，应当让新旧数字放在一起，连同各自的日期与计算方式一起留下来。
而且，岗位总数之外还会有问题：工作持续多久，工资怎样，留下来的技能能不能用于别处，公共设施能否服务更多人。这里没有足够资料替这些问题作答。把它们列出来，是提醒自己，一个合格数字并不是地方生活的全部。
政府也不该因为提供支持，就取得替每个劳动者定义前途的资格；企业则不应因接受帮助，就失去调整产品的余地。公共支持最值得争取的，是使真实的人多一些能够站稳的地方。它需要条件，但条件应该可以被说明、核查和修订，而不是要求所有人一直相信同一个宏大故事。
富士康这个案例最终留下的，或许不是一张一句话写完的成绩单。它让我们看见，支持与追问完全可以站在一起：承认今天的工作，保留对昨天的疑问，也为明天设置能够检查的边界。
答应的工作最后怎样算数？不只要有一个人数，还要让那些为这份未来付出过的人，有机会知道这个数怎样来的，并且在下一次承诺到来时，仍然能够说：请把条件摊开，我们再看看。
body_en: A promised job lives in the future. A qualifying job belongs in a particular year's records. They may eventually describe the same work, but a community should not have to treat them as interchangeable while it waits.

Foxconn's project in Wisconsin is unusually useful for thinking about that distance. There was an enormous original ambition. There were revised agreements. There is also verified investment and employment. None of these facts obliges us to call the entire undertaking either a triumph or an empty lot. The harder question is what remains open to examination as one version of the project becomes another.

The story below follows public documents through a November 2025 announcement. It is not a calculation of every public dollar associated with the site, and it does not pretend that an announcement can establish what happened after its reporting date.
## What the headline becomes in a contract

WEDC, Wisconsin's economic development agency, signed a fifteen-year agreement with Foxconn in November 2017. Its January 2019 board materials described investment of up to $10 billion, up to 13,000 jobs and as much as $2.85 billion in performance-based tax credits. That last figure was a conditional ceiling. It was not a cheque handed over at the signing ceremony.[1]

There is a serious argument for helping a large manufacturing investment get started. Equipment, training and a network of suppliers can require commitments that are difficult to coordinate one by one. Public support may make that coordination possible. Nor is a business unreasonable for wanting to know the conditions before committing its own resources. These possibilities deserve attention before we declare every incentive either necessary or corrupt.

But a headline does not tell us what the agreement actually purchases. Wisconsin's Legislative Audit Bureau examined the arrangement in report 18-18. On printed page 8, it explained that 13,000 jobs were not necessary to obtain all the available job-creation credits in the contract's final year. Its examples included 10,400 jobs at a higher average wage, alongside 13,000 at a lower one. Payroll and headcount both mattered.[1]

Those examples do not establish that anyone intended to deceive the public. They establish something simpler: the number people remember from a promise is not necessarily the threshold an administrator must enforce. A responsible assessment has to follow the promise into its operative provisions. What is mandatory, what is an upper ambition, and what can be exchanged for what?

The audit found another consequential difference. WEDC's policies said that certain unawarded job credits could not carry forward when an annual employment minimum was missed. Its contract allowed them to carry forward. The agency said it planned to alter its policies to match the contract. It would be wrong to describe that response as an audit having secured a stricter contract from Foxconn.[1]

This is not a colourful detail. It is a reminder that oversight must reach the organisation doing the checking. An agency can be sincerely trying to bring investment to a state while still needing another institution to examine how it translates an agreement into eligibility. Trust in the recipient and trust in the reviewer are different questions.

The public should be able to trace the route from a promise to a condition, from a condition to a verified result, and from that result to an award. Otherwise the most important part of an incentive agreement happens in a language accessible only to its negotiators. A larger commitment makes that route more important, not less.
## Changing a plan without changing the memory

In April 2021 Wisconsin announced a renegotiated agreement. The performance-credit ceiling became $80 million, the commitment period fell from fifteen years to six, and employment and investment targets were reset. The state's announcement also said incentives would no longer depend on manufacturing a specified product, provided the hiring and investment requirements were met.[2]

Foxconn's stated explanation was changing economic conditions and the need for flexibility in responding to market demand. Wisconsin stressed a smaller taxpayer exposure and protection of existing public investments. These arguments need not be dismissed as excuses. Orders and technologies do change. Requiring a business to preserve an obsolete production plan for the sake of an old announcement could make useful employment harder to sustain.[3]

Still, a sensible decision about what to do next cannot retrospectively establish that the original decision was sensible. There are two questions: how to use what now exists, and whether the earlier commitment was justified when it was made. A new agreement can improve the first without settling the second. Keeping both questions alive is not an insistence that the project must never change.

The governor's 2021 release described the difference between the old and new state credit ceilings as $2.77 billion in taxpayer savings. That is a comparison of potential commitments, not evidence that an equivalent sum of already-disbursed money was recovered. The same release distinguished the state credit agreement from local incentives and infrastructure investment. Reducing one ceiling did not erase every other public obligation.[2]

The opposite mistake would be to count the original ceiling as money already paid, add other costs and announce a definitive cost per job. A serious total would need separate records on land, infrastructure, finance and actual credits. This essay has not assembled that total. Declining to offer a spectacular ratio is not declining to ask what the project cost; it is refusing to disguise an incomplete account as a finished one.

An existing investment does, however, change the next decision. Something worthwhile may still be possible with facilities and skills already in place. The danger arises when that reasonable consideration turns into a permanent answer: because so much has been committed, more must always follow. Then the original decision acquires authority over every later one without being examined again.

A new round of assistance should therefore face a new question. What does this additional commitment make possible now, and what would happen without it? Asking is not wishing for a factory to close or for workers to lose their livelihood. Real livelihoods are precisely why the answer should be more careful than another repetition of the original ambition.
## The future needs its own column

WEDC's announcement of 25 November 2025 contains both a fresh expansion and a dated account of earlier activity. Start with the latter. The agency said that, as of 31 December 2024, it had verified nearly $717 million in investment and 1,242 jobs at the Mount Pleasant operation, qualifying Foxconn for $62.9 million in tax credits.[4]

That is meaningful activity under the agency's stated measure. It should not disappear merely because the original ambition was much larger. Equally, it is not another way of saying that 13,000 jobs arrived. Recognising what exists and examining the distance from an earlier promise are compatible tasks. Neither requires us to erase the other.

Dates matter as much as magnitudes. The same 2025 release described the earlier amended target as 1,454 jobs by 31 December 2025. Its verified count of 1,242 was dated a year earlier. Subtracting the latter from the former does not establish failure at the later deadline. The announcement cannot, by itself, tell us the verified year-end 2025 result.[4]

Nor does qualifying for credits establish that every corresponding dollar has already been paid. And verified employment at one employer is not proof that the incentive caused every job, or that the statewide net gain equals that count. To answer those questions, we would need evidence about what would otherwise have happened, including elsewhere in the economy. Compliance with a contract is one kind of evidence, not a complete evaluation of a policy.

Now turn to the future. The November announcement described an additional $569 million investment and 1,374 additional jobs over four years. The total performance-credit ceiling would rise to $96 million through the end of 2029, with a stated total job target of 2,616. Those are commitments and proposed activity for the new stage. They should not be folded into the preceding verified figures as completed results.[4]

An announcement understandably points forward. An accountable public record must also remain readable backwards. If each new target displaces the previous one, the public is repeatedly invited to a departure and never given a clear account of the journey just completed. A useful update keeps both columns: what was expected, and what has been checked, each with its own date and definition.

Headcount is not the whole local story either. How long do the jobs last? What do people earn? Can acquired skills be used elsewhere? Can the infrastructure support a wider range of activity? The documents reviewed here do not answer all of that. Leaving these questions visible prevents a qualifying count from standing in for everything a community might reasonably care about.

Public support should not entitle a government to define every worker's future. Accepting it should not make a firm incapable of changing a product. The point of conditions is to make assistance answerable, not to freeze everyone inside one prediction. A workable arrangement leaves room for adaptation while preserving a record against which adaptation can be judged.

There is no need to choose between acknowledging today's work and retaining yesterday's questions. We can ask what an investment made possible, what it failed to deliver, and what a revised commitment should require. Those questions do not become disloyal when people have a livelihood at stake. They become more important.

When do promised jobs count? When there is work to count, certainly. But also when the people who helped finance the promise can understand the measure, question the assessment, and meet the next offer without being told that the previous commitment has already decided their answer.
